Eloquence
ĕl´ō-kwĕns
n. (the power of speaking well; oratory that moves as well as informs)
Latin eloquentia, from eloqui, to speak out. Scripture has an eloquent preacher (Apollos), an inarticulate one (Moses), and one who deliberately declined the art (Paul).

Biblical Definition

Eloquence is skill in speech. Scripture presents it three ways and blesses none of them absolutely. Apollos “an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus” and was still taught “the way of God more perfectly” by a tentmaker and his wife (Act 18:24–26). Moses pleads the opposite: “O my Lord, I am not eloquent… but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exo 4:10), and is sent anyway. Paul declines the art on purpose: “I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom” (1Co 2:1), because the gospel is not preached “with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect” (1Co 1:17). His critics said “his speech contemptible” (2Co 10:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines eloquence as oratory; the art or the act of speaking with fluency, elegance and force, so as to please, affect and persuade.

expand to see more

ELOQUENCE, n. Oratory; the art or the act of speaking with fluency, elegance and force, so as to please, affect and persuade.

Eloquence is not merely the power of speaking well, but of speaking so as to command attention, to move the passions, and to persuade the will.

ELOQUENT, a. Having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation.

Key Scripture

Act 18:24 — "And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus."

Exo 4:10 — "And Moses said unto the LORD, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue."

1Co 2:1 — "And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God."

1Co 1:17 — "For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect."

2Co 10:10 — "For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible."

Modern Corruption

The gift is treated as the qualification for ministry, and Paul refused to use his and Moses did not have one.

expand to see more

First Corinthians 1:17 gives the reason for the refusal and it is a reason about causation, not taste: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect. Eloquence can produce every visible sign of a work of God — tears, decisions, a full room, a moved congregation — without the Spirit doing anything, and that is its danger. A church cannot easily tell, from the outside, whether it was persuaded or converted, and neither can the man in the pulpit. Paul's remedy was to remove the variable.

It does not follow that plainness is a virtue in itself, and Scripture will not support the preacher who mistakes being dull for being faithful. God gave Apollos his gifts, Luke commends them, and the same Apollos watered where Paul planted. The book of Isaiah is magnificent prose, the Psalms are poetry, and the Lord's parables are the most memorable short fiction ever composed. The question is what the skill is serving. Eloquence spent on making the text clear and its weight felt is a gift returned; eloquence spent on making the speaker admired is what Corinth was buying.

Exodus 4 is the encouragement for the other kind of man, and God's answer to Moses is worth reading exactly: Who hath made man's mouth?… have not I the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say. He does not grant the excuse and He does not supply eloquence; He supplies Himself. Moses remained slow of speech and led a nation out of Egypt, and the words he eventually wrote have outlasted every orator of the ancient world.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek logios (G3052), eloquent, learned; huperoche logou (G5247, G3056), excellency of speech; sophia logou (G4678), wisdom of words; Hebrew kebad peh (H3515, H6310), heavy of mouth.

expand to see more

Greek logios (G3052) — eloquent, learned; Acts 18:24 only.

Greek sophia logou (G4678 with G3056) — wisdom of words; 1 Corinthians 1:17, 2:1, 2:4.

Hebrew kebad peh ukebad lashon (H3515) — slow of speech and of a slow tongue; Exodus 4:10.

Usage

"“Lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect” — the reason for the refusal."

"“I am not eloquent” — and he was sent anyway."

"“His speech contemptible” — said of Paul, by Corinthians."
